title: Inside Meta’s push to put robots to work in data centers
gist: Meta is quietly testing robots from Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB to handle cabling, power-cycling, and server maintenance inside its data centers, aiming to cut labor costs as AI infrastructure spending soars, while workers describe declining job quality and fear of replacement.

insights.claim: Meta is testing robots and related hardware from Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB to perform physical data center tasks including power cycling servers, swapping networking cables, and reseating parts.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Signals Meta is actively piloting multiple robotics vendors simultaneously for core data center operations, a leading indicator of where AI-infra capex may shift from labor to automation hardware.

insights.claim: A Meta data center worker estimates that if a robot being tested to swap networking cables succeeds, it could replace up to 80 percent of some employees' physical-task workloads.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: An 80% workload-replacement estimate for cabling tasks quantifies the scale of potential headcount reduction in data center operations if the pilot scales.
insights.quote: We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore. It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.
insights.locator: paragraph on Kinova Gen3 arm and cable-swap robot

insights.claim: At some Meta facilities, a simple finger-like robot is used to remotely press the power button on a Mac Mini or other device to restart it when prompted by a human.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Even trivial physical-automation tasks are being solved first, showing Meta is building a ladder of robotics use cases from simplest to most complex.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'At some facilities, Meta quietly adopted'

insights.claim: Eric Xu, Meta's senior manager for robotics, said at a conference last year that the company's long-term goal is to put robots in data centers to speed incident response, monitor the environment, and handle preventative maintenance.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Confirms robotics is a stated strategic priority for Meta's infrastructure org, not just an isolated experiment.
insights.quote: We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start, otherwise we don’t have a chance to do this.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'But at a conference last year'

insights.claim: Data center robots historically crushed servers during simple tasks and were too expensive to deploy widely, but falling hardware costs and much more capable AI models have recently made them commercially viable.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The cost/capability inflection point explains why data-center robotics is suddenly attracting Meta, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon simultaneously rather than being a fringe experiment.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Until recently, robots largely weren't well suited'

insights.claim: Robots can offer more consistent output at lower cost than human labor in data centers, particularly in less populous regions where facilities are plentiful but qualified technicians are scarce.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Labor-scarce regions with heavy data center buildout are the likely first markets for robotic labor substitution, a factor investors should weight in siting decisions.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Robots could offer more consistent output'

insights.claim: Removing human workers from data centers could eventually make it more feasible to operate facilities in extreme environments such as underwater or in space.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A longer-horizon, speculative implication: full robotic operation removes the human-habitability constraint on data center siting, potentially unlocking novel infrastructure geographies.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Robots could offer more consistent output'

insights.claim: Analog Devices' Paul Golding, who oversees the company's physical intelligence unit, says customers increasingly want to run data centers with humanoid robots because robots can operate at higher temperatures and in the dark.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Robotic tolerance for heat and darkness could relax cooling and lighting requirements, changing data center design economics beyond just labor cost.
insights.quote: More and more of our customers are telling us ‘we want to run our data centers using humanoid [robots]’ because you can run them at higher temperatures, in the dark, and all these things.

themes.theme: Labor, tax breaks, and political blind spot

insights.claim: The nationwide activist movement against data centers has paid little attention to the growing use of robots inside them, even though tech companies routinely cite local job creation to justify tax breaks for these facilities.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: If robots hollow out the jobs used to justify tax incentives, local governments' cost-benefit case for those breaks weakens over time, creating future political and fiscal risk for the industry.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The growing use of robots has received little attention'

insights.claim: Meta's Altoona, Iowa data center campus, opened in 2014, employs hundreds of workers and still has several years left on a property tax break saving the company tens of millions of dollars annually, a trade-off the city has viewed as worthwhile for the Meta jobs it brought.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Quantifies the fiscal stakes for local governments if robotic automation reduces the headcount that justified the original tax deal.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'In Altoona, Iowa, Meta operates'

insights.claim: Meta data center workers in Altoona have grown demoralized, with group chats discussing the belief that most of them will be gone within a few years because of robots.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Internal worker sentiment already reflects an assumption of near-term displacement, which could show up in retention, unionization pressure, or local political backlash before robots are fully deployed.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'In Altoona, Meta worker group chats'

insights.claim: Two Meta workers say the company is developing AI software and other technology that will let it hire lower-skilled, lower-paid workers and centralize more complex roles in cheaper markets such as Denver, Colorado.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Suggests the near-term labor effect of AI/robotics in data centers may be wage and skill-tier compression before full headcount reduction, a distinct margin lever from outright job elimination.
insights.quote: They no longer want people who can think independently, come up with creative solutions, or perform complex troubleshooting. They want ‘smart hands,’ people who are just capable enough to follow AI instructions and not mess anything up.
insights.locator: quote from Meta data center worker on 'smart hands'

insights.claim: In response to automation concerns, Meta launched a free, long-term training program in electrical, mechanical, and plumbing skills, guaranteeing employment in states including Louisiana, Ohio, Indiana, and Texas, and partnered with building trade unions on apprenticeships.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Meta is proactively managing the political optics of automation with visible worker-training commitments, likely to preempt the tax-break and community-relations risk described elsewhere in the piece.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Meta contends its need for skilled workers'

themes.theme: Industry-wide robotics race and current limitations

insights.claim: Microsoft and Google both announced investments in data center robotics after Meta's 2023 tugger-robot rollout, and Amazon has discussed using robots to help recycle parts at its facilities.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Data center robotics is becoming a competitive, industry-wide capex category among the largest hyperscalers, not a Meta-only bet.

insights.claim: Microsoft's Ashley Llorens, a managing director at its research accelerator, confirmed the company is actively pursuing robotics for economically valuable tasks such as replacing a faulty server rack.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Direct confirmation from a Microsoft research leader validates that hyperscaler robotics investment is deliberate and tied to specific cost-saving use cases, not speculative PR.
insights.quote: absolutely something we’re looking into at Microsoft

insights.claim: Meta's existing tugger and inventory robots, deployed in Iowa and Virginia, still have significant limitations: the inventory bot's grayscale camera cannot distinguish red from green indicator lights, it struggles with corners and cables, and it is considered too slow, with drones explored as an alternative but ultimately not pursued.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Shows current-generation data center robots still require substantial human backup, indicating full labor replacement is further off than headline robotics announcements suggest.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The inventory bot is now also being used'

insights.claim: Watney Robotics pivoted from a 2023 laundry-folding and janitorial robot demo to focus on data center robots in early 2025, and its dual-armed robots have been tested on cabling work at Meta's Altoona facility since last June under human supervision, working slower than people but showing promise.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A robotics startup reallocating from general consumer/janitorial robotics to the data-center vertical signals where founders and investors see the nearest-term commercial demand for physical AI.

insights.claim: Exclaim Robotics CEO Helen Oleynikova cautions that despite many pilots and demos in data center robotics, there is no proven working solution yet.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A robotics-industry insider's skepticism is a useful counterweight to hyperscaler PR, suggesting near-term revenue and margin impact from data-center robotics should be discounted for execution risk.
insights.quote: There’s been a lot of pilots and demos, but no provable working solution.

insights.claim: Meta has internally acknowledged that current robots cannot handle the intense cabling work required to run an Nvidia GB300 supercomputer, because data center hardware has been designed for human hands for decades and would need to be redesigned for automation.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Cutting-edge AI compute clusters like Nvidia's GB300 are currently a hard limit on robotic automation, meaning the most capex-intensive, highest-value part of the data center may stay human-labor-dependent the longest.
insights.quote: Things have been designed for human hands forever to make everything a five-minute repair. Redesigning everything will take time.
insights.locator: final paragraph, quote from former Meta employee
